subtopic_detail: recognising sight threatening orbitopathy when the thyroid biochemistry has already been corrected
stem:
You are the medical registrar seeing a 46 year old woman in the emergency department. She has been taking carbimazole for three months for hyperthyroidism and her most recent clinic bloods were reported as satisfactory.

For the past two weeks the vision in her right eye has been blurred, and this week she noticed that a red traffic light looks washed out and grey compared with how it appears through the left eye. She has forward protrusion of both eyes and cannot look up fully on the right. She is a current smoker of fifteen cigarettes daily.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral proptosis with lid retraction, restricted elevation of the right eye, right relative afferent pupillary defect, red desaturation in the right eye, corneas intact
data_table.Investigations: Visual acuity 6/18 right and 6/6 left, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, free thyroxine within normal limits, free triiodothyronine within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Increase the carbimazole dose and review in the clinic in four weeks
options.rationale: Her thyroid function tests are already within normal limits, so there is no residual thyrotoxicosis to treat, and the orbitopathy runs a course partly independent of the biochemistry. Escalating the antithyroid drug risks hypothyroidism, which itself worsens eye disease. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Refer the same day for intravenous methylprednisolone under ophthalmology
options.rationale: Reduced acuity with a relative afferent pupillary defect and red desaturation indicates optic nerve compromise, which is the sight threatening form of the disease and a medical emergency. High dose intravenous corticosteroid is the immediate treatment, with orbital decompression if the response is inadequate within one to two weeks. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Prescribe lubricant eye drops and review in the clinic in six weeks
options.rationale: Ocular surface lubrication is the right supportive measure for mild disease with grittiness and exposure symptoms. It does nothing for compression of the optic nerve at the orbital apex, and a six week delay in that setting risks permanent loss. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists

options.text: Refer for radioactive iodine ablation of the thyroid within two weeks
options.rationale: Radioiodine is relatively contraindicated while the orbitopathy is active because it can precipitate deterioration, and where it is unavoidable it is given under corticosteroid cover. Choosing it as the response to failing vision inverts the priority. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Refer for routine orbital radiotherapy at the next available appointment
options.rationale: Orbital radiotherapy has a place in moderate to severe active disease, usually in combination with corticosteroid, but its effect develops over weeks to months. A routine referral does not match the tempo of an optic neuropathy. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists

explanation.summary: Thyroid associated orbitopathy is driven by autoantibody mediated inflammation of orbital fat and extraocular muscle and follows its own active then inactive course, which is why it can progress or first appear after the thyroid biochemistry has been normalised. Severity is graded by the impact on sight, and the two sight threatening manifestations are compressive optic neuropathy from apical muscle crowding and corneal breakdown from failure of lid closure. Reduced acuity, a relative afferent pupillary defect, impaired colour vision with red desaturation and optic disc swelling are the findings that define the emergency, and they must be sought explicitly because proptosis severity correlates poorly with nerve compromise. Smoking is the strongest modifiable risk factor for progression and for treatment failure, so cessation support is part of the management rather than an aside. Both hyperthyroidism and hypothyroidism worsen the eye disease, so restoring and maintaining euthyroidism matters even though it does not by itself treat the orbit.
key_points: Orbitopathy can progress after the thyroid biochemistry has normalised
Relative afferent pupillary defect and red desaturation define compressive optic neuropathy
High dose intravenous methylprednisolone is the immediate treatment, with decompression for non response
Smoking is the strongest modifiable driver of progression and treatment failure
Radioiodine can worsen active eye disease and needs corticosteroid cover if unavoidable
explanation.pearls: Loss of red colour saturation tested by asking the patient to compare a red object between the two eyes detects optic nerve compression in thyroid eye disease before visual acuity falls, and it takes about thirty seconds at the bedside.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists

subtopic_detail: interpreting a normal random growth hormone in suspected somatotroph excess and choosing the screening test
stem:
You are the endocrinology registrar reviewing a 48 year old man referred with a two year history of headaches and increasing daytime sleepiness. A sleep study last year showed obstructive sleep apnoea and he uses continuous positive airway pressure.

He tells you that his wedding ring had to be cut off last year and that he has gone up three shoe sizes since his thirties. He has noticed new gaps appearing between his lower teeth and his dentist has remarked on the change in his bite. He has bilateral hand tingling that wakes him at night. His referring doctor has already sent one blood test.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, blood pressure 156/94, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 96 per cent in air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Coarse facial features with prominent supraorbital ridges, macroglossia, spade like hands, bilateral positive Tinel sign at the wrists, visual fields full to confrontation
data_table.Investigations: Random serum growth hormone 1.8 mIU/L, glycated haemoglobin 7.2 per cent (less than 6.0), fasting glucose 7.4 mmol/L (3.0 to 5.4), calcium within normal limits, prolactin within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Repeat the random serum growth hormone level on three separate mornings
options.rationale: Growth hormone is secreted in pulses with troughs that reach undetectable levels even in active disease, so a random value cannot exclude the condition however many times it is repeated. This is the reasoning trap that the single normal result sets. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Oral glucose tolerance test with serial growth hormone measurements
options.rationale: Failure of growth hormone to suppress after a glucose load is the confirmatory test, and it is the correct next step only once the screening result is raised or equivocal. Running it before the screening test reverses the established sequence and uses a more demanding test than the situation requires. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia)

options.text: Measure serum insulin like growth factor 1 against an age matched range
options.rationale: Insulin like growth factor 1 integrates growth hormone exposure over days and has a long half life, so it is stable across the day and is the screening test of choice. The result must be read against an age and sex matched reference range because normal values fall with age. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia)

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary fossa with contrast now
options.rationale: Imaging follows biochemical confirmation rather than preceding it, because incidental pituitary lesions are found in around one in ten adults and a scan done first cannot distinguish a functioning tumour from an incidentaloma. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Measure 24 hour urinary free cortisol on two separate collections
options.rationale: Cortisol excess can also produce hypertension, glucose intolerance and changed facial appearance, which makes it a reasonable differential to hold. It does not explain acral enlargement, increasing shoe size, dental separation or macroglossia, which are specific to growth hormone excess. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Somatotroph excess develops insidiously over years and the diagnosis is typically delayed by close to a decade, so the presenting complaints are usually its complications rather than the appearance itself. Obstructive sleep apnoea, carpal tunnel syndrome, hypertension, glucose intolerance, arthropathy and colonic polyps cluster together and should raise suspicion when they appear in combination in middle age. The biochemical pathway is fixed: insulin like growth factor 1 is the screening test because it reflects integrated secretion, a glucose load with serial growth hormone measurement is the confirmatory test, and pituitary imaging comes last to localise the source once the biochemistry is established. The excess mortality is largely cardiovascular and is reversed when the growth hormone axis is controlled, which is why finding the diagnosis matters even after years of slow change. Transsphenoidal surgery is first line treatment, with somatostatin analogues, dopamine agonists and growth hormone receptor antagonists for residual disease.
key_points: A normal random growth hormone never excludes somatotroph excess because secretion is pulsatile
Insulin like growth factor 1 read against an age matched range is the screening test
Growth hormone suppression after an oral glucose load is the confirmatory test
Image the pituitary only after the biochemistry is established
Sleep apnoea, carpal tunnel syndrome, hypertension and glucose intolerance cluster as presenting complications
explanation.pearls: Ask the patient whether their ring size or shoe size has changed in adulthood and whether gaps have appeared between the teeth; acral and jaw change over years is more discriminating than facial appearance, which the treating doctor and family both adapt to gradually.

subtopic_detail: interpreting a markedly raised ferritin when the transferrin saturation is normal
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 52 year old man who came in for a fatigue check. He works long hours, sleeps poorly and has gained weight steadily since his forties. His body mass index is 33 kg/m2 and his waist circumference is 112 cm.

He has type 2 diabetes managed on metformin. He drinks four standard drinks a week and has done so for years. There is no family history of liver disease and no arthralgia, and he has no skin pigmentation change. His initial blood results have come back and his general practice colleague has flagged the ferritin.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 146/90, remaining vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 33 kg/m2, waist circumference 112 cm, no hepatomegaly, no stigmata of chronic liver disease, no skin bronzing
data_table.Investigations: Ferritin 980 micrograms/L (30 to 300), transferrin saturation 31 per cent (15 to 45), alanine aminotransferase 78 U/L (less than 40), aspartate aminotransferase 52 U/L (less than 35), C reactive protein within normal limits, full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Send HFE genotyping for the C282Y and H63D variants before anything else
options.rationale: Genotyping is indicated when the transferrin saturation is persistently raised, conventionally above about 45 per cent, because saturation rather than ferritin is the marker of true iron loading. A saturation of 31 per cent makes hereditary iron overload very unlikely and a positive genotype here would more likely be an incidental carrier state than the explanation. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia)

options.text: Begin weekly therapeutic venesection and recheck the ferritin at ten weeks
options.rationale: Venesection treats established iron overload, which has not been demonstrated. Removing blood will lower the ferritin in almost anyone, so the falling number would falsely appear to confirm a diagnosis he does not have while the actual liver disease goes unaddressed. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging for hepatic iron quantification now
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance iron quantification is an accurate non invasive measure and is the right test when iron overload is genuinely suspected but the biochemistry is ambiguous. Ordering it when the saturation is normal spends a scarce resource on a question the saturation has already answered. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists

options.text: Arrange liver ultrasound with viral serology and fasting iron studies
options.rationale: Ferritin is an acute phase protein that rises with hepatic inflammation, adiposity, insulin resistance and alcohol, and with a normal saturation the raised value is far more likely to reflect one of these than iron loading. Imaging the liver, excluding viral hepatitis and repeating iron studies fasting addresses the probable causes and the transaminase rise together. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia)

options.text: Refer for percutaneous liver biopsy to quantify the hepatic iron index
options.rationale: Biopsy has largely been displaced by genotyping and magnetic resonance quantification for the assessment of iron, and it carries a small risk of significant bleeding. It may still have a role later for staging fibrosis, but it is not the step that follows this result. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia)

explanation.summary: A raised ferritin is one of the commonest abnormal results in Australian general practice and the great majority of raised values do not represent iron overload. Ferritin behaves as an acute phase reactant and rises with inflammation, infection, malignancy, alcohol use, hepatocellular injury and the insulin resistant state, so the result must always be read alongside the transferrin saturation, which is the marker that actually tracks body iron stores. Persistent saturation above about 45 per cent is the threshold that prompts HFE genotyping, whereas a normal saturation with a raised ferritin redirects the workup toward liver disease, alcohol and metabolic factors. Dysmetabolic iron overload syndrome describes the pattern of modestly raised ferritin with normal saturation in the setting of metabolic syndrome, and it is managed by treating the metabolic drivers rather than by venesection. Where transaminases are also raised, the assessment must proceed to imaging, viral serology and a fibrosis estimate, because the fibrosis stage is what determines prognosis.
key_points: Transferrin saturation, not ferritin, is the marker of true iron loading
Ferritin rises with inflammation, adiposity, insulin resistance, alcohol and hepatocyte injury
Genotype only when the saturation is persistently above about 45 per cent
Venesection lowers ferritin in anyone and can falsely appear to confirm the wrong diagnosis
A raised transaminase alongside a raised ferritin needs imaging, viral serology and fibrosis staging
explanation.pearls: Repeat iron studies fasting before acting on them, because transferrin saturation rises after a meal and after iron supplements and can push a normal result above the 45 per cent genotyping threshold on a non fasting sample.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists
